newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices rise, coffee and lumber tumble.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices rise, coffee and lumber tumble.

text.p: Oil prices rose Thursday as traders shrugged off a possible extension of Iraqi oil sales amid expectations of tighter heating oil supplies and colder weather.
Coffee prices weakened on talk that a leading coffee consultant in Brazil forecast next season's crop would be higher than recent estimates.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, February heating oil closed 1.50 cents a gallon higher at 70.34 cents, and February unleaded gasoline rose 1.59 cents a gallon at 69.82 cents.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan told a a news conference in Geneva the current U.N. deal allowing Iraq to sell oil to buy food could be extended.
"My expectation is now that we are beginning the scheme, it will continue to be extended another six months," he said.

In December, the United Nations eased Gulf War sanctions against Iraq to allow it to sell $2 billion worth of oil for six months in exchange for humanitarian aid. The sanctions were imposed following Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
But, countering the prospect of more Iraqi crude in the pipeline were several near-term factors that prompted buying.

Two of Mexico's largest crude oil export ports, Pajaritos and Dos Bocas, remained shut for a third day Thursday by strong winds that closed four ports in the Gulf of Mexico. The two crude oil ports handle 850,000 barrels of oil per day.
Traders also said seasonal refinery maintenance continued to diminish heating oil and gasoline output. In addition, weather forecasts pointed to a boost in heating oil demand.
The National Weather Service's six-to-10-day forecast for the Feb. 4-8 period issued Wednesday predicted below-normal temperatures in the Northeast.
March crude closed up 40 cents at $24.87 a barrel.

At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, the coffee market took a break from a rally that has sent prices up 40 percent in two months. March coffee closed 4.30 cents a pound lower at 140.30 cents.
"The market was expecting a correction," said Refco coffee analyst Ann Prendergast. "It had gone up significantly and was due for a retracement in order to sustain the upsurge."

Traders said today's sell-off was sparked by talk that a leading coffee consultant in Brazil, the No. 1 exporting country, forecast next season's crop would come in well above a string of recent estimates.
Talk that consultant Leon Yallouz pegged the 1997/98 Brazil crop at more than 27 million bags in a preliminary estimate based on field trips in September weighed on the market.

That estimate, unconfirmed by Yallouz, would differ sharply from preliminary estimates by Brazil's government, which pegged the coming crop at 18 million to 20 million bags. Brazil harvested about 25 million 132-pound bags a year ago.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, March lumber futures closed down the $10 allowable daily limit at $401.80 per thousand board feet as cash lumber quotes weakened.

Reports of wholesalers holding asking prices at $390, well under mill levels, prompted renewed pressure. Continued concern over the amount of lumber arriving under voluntary quotas from Canada also prompted speculative selling.

"(Canadian) mills are going to have to discount their prices to make make sure their full allocations are sold. Otherwise, they lose their allocations for next year," said Neil Schmaedick, Smith Barney forest products analyst.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, heavy selling in soybeans led grain markets lower. March soybeans closed 8-1/2 cents lower at $7.41-1/2.
Rains in Brazil's southern soybean growing regions sent soybean futures tumbling, as did weak exports.
"There was more rain and the exports weren't very good," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter. "All that's weighing on beans, and beans are pulling everything else down."
The Agriculture Department in weekly data Thursday reported soybean export sales of 348,700 metric tons, near the bottom of trade expectations for 300,000 to 500,000 tons.

The selling weighed on corn prices, where March corn ended 1-1/4 cents a bushel lower at $2.73-3/4 despite weekly export sales of 1.285 million tons, above expectations for bookings of 800,000 to 1 million tons.
